\label{sec:violation_landscape}

We evaluate OntoCoDec in two deployment configurations.
LoRA + greedy S1 (\S\ref{sec:composability}) is the recommended fast configuration, near-eliminating DR violations with minimal latency overhead.
LoRA + beam S1 (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}) additionally resolves cross-field consistency, achieving zero total violations at 1.54$\times$ latency.
Zero-shot evaluation (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}--\S\ref{sec:cross-model}) isolates layer contributions as a diagnostic; R-F1 2--8 reflects the absence of task-specific training, not method failure.

\paragraph{Setup.}
We evaluate on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} (551 test sentences, 7 relations, $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$) and DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} (998 dev documents,\footnote{DocRED test annotations are not publicly available; we evaluate on the development set.} 96 relations, $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$).
RE type constraints are extracted automatically from observed type pairs in training data (neither dataset provides a formal ontology); EE constraints on WikiEvents (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}) are derived from the KAIROS ontology.
The framework handles both sources without modification.
Primary model: Qwen3-8B~\cite{qwen2025qwen3}, zero-shot greedy decoding; cross-model validation in \S\ref{sec:cross-model}, composability with fine-tuning in \S\ref{sec:composability}.
We measure four violation categories: \textbf{DR} (domain/range type pair $\notin \sigma(r)$), \textbf{RV} (relation $\notin \mathcal{R}$), \textbf{ET} (entity type $\notin \mathcal{E}$), and \textbf{CF} (same entity assigned conflicting types across triples).
Baseline DR violations are 15.37\% (SciERC) and 18.46\% (DocRED), comparable rates associated with constraint tightness rather than ontology scale (\S\ref{sec:introduction}); schema-informed prompting reduces DR by 62\% on SciERC but is per-relation unreliable (Appendix~\ref{app:per-relation-landscape}).

\label{app:reproducibility}

\paragraph{Fine-tuning configuration.}

All runs use seed 42.

\paragraph{Hardware and software.}
Training runs on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU (98\,GB VRAM).

OntoCoDec guarantees levels 1--2 (grammar and semantic layers, respectively); level~3 is addressed by beam search or post-hoc resolution (Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).

\smallskip
\noindent
Existing grammar-constrained decoding frameworks (e.g., XGrammar) enforce level~1 constraints---structural validity and vocabulary membership---but IE domain/range rules require cross-position entity-type state that context-free grammars cannot express.
We formalize this gap:

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Proposition 1} (Level 2 $\not\subseteq$ Level 1)\textbf{.}
\textit{Domain/range type constraints for IE with unbounded entity sets are not context-free.}

\smallskip
\noindent\textit{Proof sketch.}
Consider $\mathcal{E} = \{\tau_A, \tau_B\}$ and a relation $r$ with $\operatorname{dom}(r) = \{\tau_A\}$.
An output contains $n$ entities with independently chosen types ($a_i \in \{A, B\}$), followed by a relation referencing head $e_k$ for arbitrary $k \leq n$.
Validating the head-type field requires retrieving $\tau_{a_k}$, the type assigned at position $k$ in the entity list.
A PDA's LIFO stack cannot retrieve position $k < n$ without destroying entries above it; since both $n$ and $k$ are independently unbounded, no PDA can enforce this constraint for all valid outputs.
OntoCoDec's semantic layer addresses this with a runtime entity registry $\mathcal{D}$ (a finite map enabling random-access type lookups), operating as a deterministic stateful transducer over the token stream.\hfill$\square$

\noindent\textbf{Corollary.} The enabling dependency is necessary: the grammar layer alone cannot enforce domain/range constraints (Proposition~1), while the semantic layer alone achieves only 24\% DR reduction without grammar-guaranteed vocabulary membership (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}, Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation}).
